claim: Dopaminergic amacrine cells (DACs) serve as the sole source of retinal dopamine.
source: Dopaminergic amacrine cells (DACs) serve as the sole source of retinal dopamine, and dopamine release in the retina follows a circadian rhythm and is modulated by light exposure.
evidence: Stated as established fact in the abstract, drawing from known scientific consensus.

claim: Dopamine release in the retina follows a circadian rhythm.
source: Dopaminergic amacrine cells (DACs) serve as the sole source of retinal dopamine, and dopamine release in the retina follows a circadian rhythm and is modulated by light exposure.
evidence: Stated as established fact, supported by citation in Introduction (Doyle et al., 2002).

claim: Dopamine release in the retina is modulated by light exposure.

claim: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) costratify with DACs in the inner plexiform layer.
source: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) have emerged as a prime target for influencing retinal dopamine levels because they costratify with DACs in the inner plexiform layer and signal to them in a retrograde manner.
evidence: Supported by citations in the Introduction (Matsuoka et al., 2011; Vugler et al., 2007).

claim: ipRGCs signal to DACs in a retrograde manner.
source: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) have emerged as a prime target for influencing retinal dopamine levels because they costratify with DACs in the inner plexiform layer and signal to them in a retrograde manner.
evidence: Supported by citations in the Introduction (Zhang et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2012).

claim: Light influences the total number of DACs.
source: Surprisingly, using genetic mouse models lacking specific phototransduction pathways, we find that while light influences the total number of DACs and retinal dopamine levels, this effect does not require ipRGCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differences in TH+ cell numbers between LD and DD conditions.

claim: Light influences retinal dopamine levels.
source: Surprisingly, using genetic mouse models lacking specific phototransduction pathways, we find that while light influences the total number of DACs and retinal dopamine levels, this effect does not require ipRGCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differences in dopamine levels between LD and DD conditions.

claim: The effect of light on DAC number does not require ipRGCs.

claim: The effect of light on retinal dopamine levels does not require ipRGCs.

claim: ipRGC dendrites co-stratify with DACs within the IPL during adulthood.

evidence: Supported by citations to Matsuoka et al., 2011; Vugler et al., 2007.

claim: Rearing in constant darkness resulted in decreased numbers of TH+ cells at P14.
source: Rearing in constant darkness resulted in decreased numbers of TH +cells at P14 (DD: Mean ± SEM = 580.8 ± 8.6 cells, n = 15 retinas; LD: Mean ± SEM = 643.7 ± 8.2 cells, n = 6 retinas; Unpaired t-test, p = 0.0004) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing DD and LD conditions at P14, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The decrease in TH+ cell number persisted when animals were dark-reared to adult stages.
source: This decrease persisted when animals were dark-reared to adult stages (DD: Mean ± SEM = 567.3 ± 10.2 cells, n = 6 retinas; LD: Mean ± SEM = 648.5 ± 17.5 cells, n = 6 retinas; One-Way ANOVA, p = 0.0002, Dunnett's multiple comparisons test) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing DD and LD conditions in adults, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The decrease in TH+ cell number in the adult retina persisted even after dark-reared mice were placed in LD at P14.
source: Interestingly, we found that this decrease in TH+ cell number in the adult retina persisted even after dark-reared mice were placed in LD at P14, demonstrating that this decrease in TH+ cell number could not be rescued by subsequent exposure to a normal LD cycle after eye opening (LD Rescue: Mean ± SEM = 541.8 ± 5.6 cells, n = 4 retinas; One-Way ANOVA, Dunnett's multiple comparisons test) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LD Rescue group, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The decrease in TH+ cell number could not be rescued by subsequent exposure to a normal LD cycle after eye opening.
source: Interestingly, we found that this decrease in TH+ cell number in the adult retina persisted even after dark-reared mice were placed in LD at P14, demonstrating that this decrease in TH+ cell number could not be rescued by subsequent exposure to a normal LD cycle after eye opening (LD Rescue: Mean ± SEM = 541.8 ± 5.6 cells, n = 4 retinas; One-Way ANOVA, Dunnett's multiple comparisons test) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LD Rescue group, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Dopamine (DA) levels were significantly reduced in DD reared animals.
source: In support of decreased TH+ cell number, dopamine (DA) levels were significantly reduced in DD reared animals (DD: Mean ± SEM = 0.6 ± 0.08 ng/mg, n = 4 retinas; LD: Mean ± SEM = 1.723 ± 0.16 ng/mg, n = 4 retinas; Unpaired t-test, p = 0.003) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing DA levels in DD and LD conditions, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: TKO retinas had significantly reduced number of TH+ cells compared to control retinas.
source: Indeed, TKO retinas had significantly reduced number of TH+ cells (TKO: Mean ± SEM = 505.0 ± 32.8 cells, n = 4 retinas; Control: Mean ± SEM = 627.4 ± 13.5 cells, n = 9 retinas; One-Way ANOVA, p < 0.0001, Dunnett's multiple comparisons test) and significantly reduced DA levels (TKO: Mean ± SEM = 2.82 ± 0.09 ng/mg, n = 6 retinas; Control: Mean ± SEM = 3.55 ± 0.22 ng/mg, n = 6 retinas; One-Way ANOVA, p < 0.0001, Dunnett's multiple comparisons test) compared to control retinas (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing TKO and Control retinas, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TKO retinas had significantly reduced DA levels compared to control retinas.
source: Indeed, TKO retinas had significantly reduced number of TH+ cells (TKO: Mean ± SEM = 505.0 ± 32.8 cells, n = 4 retinas; Control: Mean ± SEM = 627.4 ± 13.5 cells, n = 9 retinas; One-Way ANOVA, p < 0.0001, Dunnett's multiple comparisons test) and significantly reduced DA levels (TKO: Mean ± SEM = 2.82 ± 0.09 ng/mg, n = 6 retinas; Control: Mean ± SEM = 3.55 ± 0.22 ng/mg, n = 6 retinas; One-Way ANOVA, p < 0.0001, Dunnett's multiple comparisons test) compared to control retinas (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing TKO and Control retinas, shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Light is a critical modulator of TH+ cell number in the retina during development and into adulthood.
source: These results indicate that light is a critical modulator of TH+ cell number and resting DA levels in the retina during development and into adulthood.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing differences in TH+ cell numbers between LD and DD conditions.

claim: Light is a critical modulator of resting DA levels in the retina during development and into adulthood.
source: These results indicate that light is a critical modulator of TH+ cell number and resting DA levels in the retina during development and into adulthood.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing differences in DA levels between LD and DD conditions.

claim: MKO mice showed no significant change in TH+ cell number.
source: Despite reports of ipRGC influence on DA-dependent retinal physiology (Prigge et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2012; Qiao et al., 2017), we found that MKO and CKO mice showed no significant change in TH+ cell number (MKO: Mean ± SEM = 615.3±55.5 cells, n = 6 retinas; CKO: Mean ± SEM = 708.6 ± 30.74 cells, n = 9 retinas; Control Mean ± SEM = 627.4 ± 13.5 cells, n = 9 retinas; One-Way ANOVA, Dunnett's multiple comparisons test) or DA levels (MKO: Mean ± SEM = 3.63 ± 0.15 ng/mg, n = 6 retinas; CKO: Mean ± SEM = 3.88 ± 0.07 ng/mg, n = 6 retinas; Control Mean ± SEM = 3.55 ± 0.22 ng/mg, n = 6 retinas; One-Way ANOVA, Dunnett's multiple comparisons test), though CKO mice showed a trend toward increasing numbers of TH+ cells (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing MKO and Control retinas, shown in Figure 2C.

evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing CKO and Control retinas, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lack of melanopsin phototransduction does not influence basal retinal DA.
source: These data indicate that lack of melanopsin or cone phototransduction does not influence basal retinal DA as previously suggested (Dkhissi-Benyahya et al., 2013).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing no significant change in DA levels in MKO mice.

claim: Lack of cone phototransduction does not influence basal retinal DA.
source: These data indicate that lack of melanopsin or cone phototransduction does not influence basal retinal DA as previously suggested (Dkhissi-Benyahya et al., 2013).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing no significant change in DA levels in CKO mice.

claim: RKO mice showed a significant decrease in TH+ cell number.
source: Surprisingly, RKO mice showed a significant decrease in both TH+ cell number (RKO: Mean ± SEM = 518.5 ± 29.3 cells, n = 9; Control Mean ± SEM = 627.4 ± 13.5 cells, n = 9; One-Way ANOVA, p < 0.0001, Dunnett's multiple comparisons test) and DA levels (RKO: Mean ± SEM = 2.92 ± 0.09 ng/mg, n = 6 retinas; Control Mean ± SEM = 3.55 ± 0.22 ng/mg, n = 6 retinas; One-Way ANOVA, p < 0.0001, Dunnett's multiple comparisons test).

claim: RKO mice showed a significant decrease in DA levels.

evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing RKO and Control retinas, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Rods play a critical role in setting TH+ cell number in the developing and adult retina.
source: Our data from RKO tracks closely with our results from DD reared animals and TKO animals (Figure 1), indicating that rods in particular play a critical role in setting TH+ cell number and DA levels in the developing and adult retina.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing decreased TH+ cell numbers in RKO, DD, and TKO animals.

claim: Rods play a critical role in setting DA levels in the developing and adult retina.

claim: Ablation of ipRGCs did not affect the number of TH+ cells.
source: Surprisingly, ablation of ipRGCs did not affect the number of TH+ cells (DTA: Mean ± SEM = 605.2 ± 10.5 cells, n = 6 retinas; Control: Mean ± SEM = 582.6 ± 10.1 cells, n = 8 retinas; Unpaired t-test, p = 0.1522) or retinal DA levels (DTA: Mean ± SEM = 3.61 ± 0.27 ng/mg, n = 6 retinas; Control: Mean ± SEM = 3.31 ± 0.23 ng/mg, n = 6 retinas; Unpaired t-test, p = 0.4188), indicating that ipRGCs are not the relay for rod-dependent signals influencing these processes (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing DTA and Control retinas, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Ablation of ipRGCs did not affect retinal DA levels.
source: Surprisingly, ablation of ipRGCs did not affect the number of TH+ cells (DTA: Mean ± SEM = 605.2 ± 10.5 cells, n = 6 retinas; Control: Mean ± SEM = 582.6 ± 10.1 cells, n = 8 retinas; Unpaired t-test, p = 0.1522) or retinal DA levels (DTA: Mean ± SEM = 3.61 ± 0.27 ng/mg, n = 6 retinas; Control: Mean ± SEM = 3.31 ± 0.23 ng/mg, n = 6 retinas; Unpaired t-test, p = 0.4188), indicating that ipRGCs are not the relay for rod-dependent signals influencing these processes (Figure 2E–F).

claim: ipRGCs are not the relay for rod-dependent signals influencing TH+ cell number.

evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing normal TH+ cell numbers in DTA animals.

claim: ipRGCs are not the relay for rod-dependent signals influencing retinal DA levels.

claim: TH+ cell stratification appears normal in DTA retinas.
source: Additionally, we find that TH+ cell stratification also appears normal in DTA retinas, providing further support for normal DAC development in the absence of ipRGCs (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Normal DAC development occurs in the absence of ipRGCs.

evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing decreased TH+ cell numbers in RKO but not DTA animals.

claim: Rod phototransduction through non-ipRGC pathways is the critical regulator of resting retinal DA levels.

claim: Rods are the major photoreceptor class in the retina regulating the number of TH+ cells.
source: Our findings indicate that rods are the major photoreceptor class in the retina regulating the number of TH+ cells as well as resting retinal DA levels, and that they are doing so through ipRGC-independent pathways (Figure 3).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing decreased TH+ cell numbers in RKO but not MKO or CKO animals.

claim: Rods are the major photoreceptor class in the retina regulating resting retinal DA levels.

source: Cone responses, however, were detectable at lower light intensities in the dorsal versus ventral retina, while melanopsin-based responses were detectable only in the dorsal retina (Zhao et al., 2017).

claim: Melanopsin-based responses were detectable only in the dorsal retina.
source: Cone responses, however, were detectable at lower light intensities in the dorsal versus ventral retina, while melanopsin-based responses were detectable only in the dorsal retina (Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2017.

claim: Rods are the primary drivers of the defects observed in DD.
source: Our results in DD and RKO animals are roughly parallel, suggesting that rods are the primary drivers of the defects observed in DD.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of experimental data from DD and RKO animals.

claim: RKO animals have some retinal degeneration starting at 4 months.
source: RKO animals have been shown to have some retinal degeneration starting at 4 months, which could also explain the differences in magnitude (Calvert et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Calvert et al., 2000.

claim: Dark-reared animals do not have retinal degeneration.
source: This is unlikely because dark-reared animals do not have retinal degeneration, but still exhibit reduced TH+ cell number and decreased retinal DA levels (Brooks et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brooks et al., 2014 and experimental data from DD animals.

claim: Dark-reared animals exhibit reduced TH+ cell number.
source: This is unlikely because dark-reared animals do not have retinal degeneration, but still exhibit reduced TH+ cell number and decreased retinal DA levels (Brooks et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from DD animals.

claim: Dark-reared animals exhibit decreased retinal DA levels.
source: This is unlikely because dark-reared animals do not have retinal degeneration, but still exhibit reduced TH+ cell number and decreased retinal DA levels (Brooks et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from DD animals.

claim: The number of DACs is closely tied to genetic background.
source: It is also possible that these differences were due to slight genetic variability amongst cohorts because the number of DACs is closely tied to genetic background, though both of these groups were maintained on the same mixed hybrid background (see Materials and methods) (Whitney et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Whitney et al., 2009.

claim: Gnat2cpfl3/cpfl3 ('CKO') mice have been shown to retain some low sensitivity cone function.
source: Gnat2cpfl3/cpfl3 ('CKO') mice have been shown to retain some low sensitivity cone function (Chang et al., 2006), and our CKO mice showed a non-significant trend toward increased DAC number, indicating that cones may have some influence on DAC number.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chang et al., 2006.

claim: Cones may have some influence on DAC number.
source: Gnat2cpfl3/cpfl3 ('CKO') mice have been shown to retain some low sensitivity cone function (Chang et al., 2006), and our CKO mice showed a non-significant trend toward increased DAC number, indicating that cones may have some influence on DAC number.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing a trend toward increased DAC number in CKO mice.

claim: Only RKO or TKO animals recapitulated the phenotype observed in DD.
source: Nevertheless, because only RKO or TKO animals recapitulated the phenotype we observed in DD, our data argue that rods are the major pathway through which this occurs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing DD, RKO, TKO, MKO, and CKO animals.

claim: Rods are the major pathway through which light influences TH+ cell number and DA levels.
source: Nevertheless, because only RKO or TKO animals recapitulated the phenotype we observed in DD, our data argue that rods are the major pathway through which this occurs.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data comparing DD, RKO, TKO, MKO, and CKO animals.

claim: There is evidence for bidirectional signaling between DACs and ipRGCs.
source: That ipRGCs were not required for either TH+ cell number or setting retinal DA levels was surprising given the close apposition of DAC axons and ipRGC dendrites, as well as evidence for bidirectional signaling between these two populations and effects of melanopsin signaling on the number of other retinal cell types (Matsuoka et al., 2011; Vugler et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2012; Rao et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Matsuoka et al., 2011; Vugler et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2012; Rao et al., 2013.

claim: Melanopsin signaling has effects on the number of other retinal cell types.
source: That ipRGCs were not required for either TH+ cell number or setting retinal DA levels was surprising given the close apposition of DAC axons and ipRGC dendrites, as well as evidence for bidirectional signaling between these two populations and effects of melanopsin signaling on the number of other retinal cell types (Matsuoka et al., 2011; Vugler et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2012; Rao et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Matsuoka et al., 2011; Vugler et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2012; Rao et al., 2013.

claim: Previous work has shown deficits in the light adapted ERG of DTA animals that can be rescued by a D4 agonist.
source: Previous work has shown deficits in the light adapted ERG of DTA animals that can be rescued by a D4 agonist (Prigge et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Prigge et al., 2016.

claim: During development, DTA retinas show a down regulation of the D4 receptor, Drd4, which is expressed on cone photoreceptors.
source: We have found that during development, DTA retinas show a down regulation of the D4 receptor, Drd4, which is expressed on cone photoreceptors (Tufford et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tufford et al., 2018.

claim: Lack of ipRGCs may cause genetic alterations in the retina of DTA animals that makes individual cell populations in the retina less responsive to DA.
source: Therefore, it is possible that lack of ipRGCs causes genetic alterations in the retina of DTA animals that makes individual cell populations in the retina less responsive to DA.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on previous findings about Drd4 downregulation.

claim: Other currently available dopamine reporter reagents label additional and varied cell types in the retina.
source: It is important to note that while our data clearly indicate fewer TH+ cells in RKO and DD retinas, we were limited to the use of TH immunopositive cells as a proxy for DAC number because other currently available dopamine reporter reagents label additional and varied cell types in the retina (Vuong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vuong et al., 2015.

claim: In the absence of sufficient TH enzyme, any surviving DACs will be unable to functionally synthesize dopamine.
source: However, in the absence of sufficient TH enzyme, any surviving DACs will be unable to functionally synthesize dopamine.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of TH's role in dopamine synthesis.

claim: Dopamine production from a subset of DACs is lost or at least severely attenuated in DD and RKO mice.
source: Thus, though we cannot clarify the reasons for the absence of TH immunolabeling at this time, it is clear that dopamine production from a subset of DACs is lost or at least severely attenuated in DD and RKO mice.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing decreased TH+ cell numbers and DA levels in DD and RKO mice.
